node.dia-daq-read.help: Reads samples from a data acquisition task on NI hardware, through NI's gRPC Device Server. The host the hardware is attached to needs NI's DAQmx driver and the NI gRPC Device Server, started with a configuration that turns on TLS, and with an address other than localhost if Flow runs on another machine. Never leave the server's unsecured port open on a plant network: set Security to on, or to mutual to also check this node's own certificate. Finite mode takes one acquisition of the samples you set on every call. Continuous mode starts the task on the first call and reads the next block of samples on each call after it. y is the samples of one channel as an array, or an array of arrays, one per channel in order. dt is the seconds between samples. A refusal from the server or the driver is an error on the error wire with the driver's own code and text. The task is cleared on the server when the run ends. This node has been tested against a stand-in server only, not against NI's server.

node.dia-derivative.help: The slope of an array of samples at each sample, as an array the same length. Inside the array it uses the samples on both sides; at the first and last sample it uses the one neighbor it has. It needs at least two samples. The time between samples comes from the dt input in seconds, else the rate input in hertz, else the Samples per second property. Differentiating amplifies noise, so filter a noisy signal first.
node.dia-derivative.prop.rate.label: Samples per second
node.dia-field.help: Takes one field out of a record. With a shared type named, deploy says so when the type has no such field.
node.dia-field.prop.field.label: Field
node.dia-field.prop.shape.label: Shared type (optional)
node.dia-filter.help: A Butterworth filter: flat in the band it passes, with no ripple, and 3 dB down at the cutoff. Lowpass keeps what is slower than the cutoff, highpass keeps what is faster, bandpass keeps what is between the two edges, and bandstop removes it. A higher order cuts off more sharply and rings a little longer after a step. The cutoff must be above zero and below half the sample rate. Give it an array, or one number at a time, and it remembers where it was between calls in a run, so a signal cut into pieces is filtered as one. The rate input wins over the Samples per second property. It starts from rest, so the first samples of an array carry a start-up settle; it delays the signal by an amount that depends on frequency, so it is wrong to use where the timing between two signals has to line up exactly; and it is not a linear-phase or zero-phase filter.

A number is stored as a 64 bit float, a true or false as a bool, and anything else as text. A column that holds a list of numbers adds all of them, which is how a block of samples goes in. The properties are written on the file when the run starts. A file that already exists is appended to, so runs follow each other in one file, and a file cut short by a power loss is repaired to its last complete row before the new rows go on. With write to disk on, a power cut loses at most the row being written. It can start a new file when this one reaches a size or an age and keep only the newest finished files: bench.tdms becomes bench-20261114T120000Z.tdms and the log goes on in bench.tdms, with the file properties written again. node.dia-stable.help: Says whether the last readings agree. node.dia-wave-parts.help: Takes a waveform apart: its samples, the seconds between them, when the first was taken (as text), how long it spans (the samples times the step), how many samples it holds and its attributes.

node.exec.compat: The three outputs, both buffered and streaming modes, the timeout and the appended message property all behave as Node-RED's do. Two things do not, and neither is negotiable. There is no shell: the command line is split on quoting rules only, and an unquoted shell metacharacter is refused rather than run, so one allowed command cannot become an arbitrary one. And the node is disabled until an operator names the commands a flow may run. Node-RED's exec node runs anything, and Node-RED starts with no authentication by default; a vendor shipping that default became CVE-2025-41656 (Pilz IndustrialPI 4, VDE-2025-045), unauthenticated command execution on the device. Output is capped per stream; a command that exceeds it is killed and reported rather than being allowed to fill the heap. A command that forks children of its own may leave them behind when it is killed.

node.function.compat: Runs on goja, a JavaScript interpreter written in Go, rather than Node's vm module. The language is ES2023; the Node standard library is not present. require() and npm modules do not work and cannot be made to without embedding Node. There is always a CPU time limit, which Node-RED leaves optional and off, and it applies to every timer callback too. setTimeout, setInterval and their clear functions work, on the node's clock, and every one is cleared when the flow stops or is redeployed. Buffer is there (alloc, from, concat, the read and write methods for integers and floats in both byte orders, slice, toString and toJSON). A byte slice in a message arrives as a byte array, so wrap it with Buffer.from. await works at the top level of the body, a promise the body returns is waited for, a promise the Setup code returns is settled before the first message runs, and node.linkcall(target, msg, {timeout, clone}) calls a Link In by id or name and resolves with what its Link Out in return mode sends back (5 second wait unless the call says otherwise).

node.http in.compat: Serves a path, with Express-style :params and a trailing *, and builds the same msg.req / msg.res / msg.payload shape Node-RED does, including JSON, form-encoded and raw bodies. Three deliberate differences. A request that no HTTP Response node answers is closed with 504 after a timeout instead of being held open forever, because Node-RED's version leaks a connection per request until the process runs out of sockets and stops answering with nothing in the log. Two nodes claiming the same method and path is refused at deploy time rather than one of them silently never firing. And a path that would shadow the editor or the admin API is refused for the same reason. Uploads parse the way multer does in Node-RED: text fields into msg.payload, files into msg.req.files, a broken upload answered with 500. One bound multer lacks: an array index over 10,000 in a field name, a[99999999], is refused instead of building a sparse array that long. msg.req.cookies is cookie-parser's, j: values included.

node.http request.compat: Method, URL, headers, basic authentication, redirects and the three return types, with msg.url, msg.method and msg.headers overriding the node. The response body is size-capped and the call is bounded by a timeout, neither of which Node-RED does. TLS comes from a tls-config, or without one msg.rejectUnauthorized = false skips the certificate check for that one message, as in Node-RED. msg.cookies and a cookie header go out through a cookie jar, cookies a redirect sets follow the redirect, and msg.responseCookies and msg.redirectList come back, all as in Node-RED. The path shares the flow route table with the HTTP In nodes, so it cannot shadow the editor or the admin API and cannot collide with another node's path. A client that stops reading is disconnected rather than queued without limit, which Node-RED does not do.

node.xml.compat: Both directions, using xml2js's object convention: attributes under the key named by "attr" (default $), element text under "chr" (default _), and every child element as an array, which is xml2js's own explicitArray default. Set ew_explicitArray to false to collapse single children instead. The per-message msg.options that Node-RED passes through to xml2js is not honoured — the other xml2js options change the shape of the output, and silently ignoring one would produce an object the flow does not expect while looking like it worked. Namespaces are kept as part of the element name rather than being resolved.
